clue.text: More sage is planted in middle of flowerbed

indicators.note: something planted in a bed is set inside it, so one piece goes into another
the central three letters of the word flowerbed are taken

explanation.surface: A gardener sets more sage into the centre of a flowerbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sage' looks like the herb in a flowerbed, but it is the adjective meaning wise; 'middle of' here takes the central three letters, not one.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage means wise, so 'more sage' is the comparative, wiser.

clue.text: Using support to hold one's ground

parts.note: with can mean using, as in cut with a knife
a stand is a support

explanation.surface: Leaning on something to stay firm.
explanation.definitionFit: To withstand is to resist, holding firm against an attack.

clue.text: Wise man goes around America in a banger

indicators.note: goes around means encircles, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a sage is a wise man
USA, the United States of America

explanation.surface: A wise man drives around America in an old car.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'banger' is British slang both for a sausage and for a clapped-out car, which the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Banger is British slang for a sausage, from its habit of bursting in the pan.

clue.text: Decorated all over again, using colour I had

parts.note: red is a colour
I'd contracts I had

explanation.surface: Someone repaints a room in a colour they once chose.
explanation.definitionFit: If you redid a room you decorated it once more.

clue.text: Sectional management of seaboard

parts.note: line management is the running of a business section by section; applied to the shore, the line that marks out the sea's edge is the phrase meant

explanation.surface: A dry phrase from an organisation chart about running a coastal authority in sections.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like business jargon (line management by section), but the 'line' is the boundary where land meets sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaboard's edge, the shore line along the land, is described as if it were a management line.

clue.text: Confirmed account of events the French rejected

indicators.note: rejected means thrown out, so the French word for the is removed

parts.note: a chronicle is a record of events
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A verified history that the French refused to accept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confirmed' as in a confirmed bachelor: habitual, long-standing.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronic condition or habit is long-standing and ingrained, as a confirmed one is.

clue.text: Bearing left for Luton, say

parts.note: air means bearing or manner
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Directions telling a driver to bear left for the town of Luton.
explanation.walkthrough: Luton, north of London, has an airport; the surface reads 'Bearing left' as a driving direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Luton has a well-known London airport, so it is an example; 'say' signals that.

clue.text: Drummer boy is employed in seasonal entertainment, mostly

parts.note: Tim is a boy's name

indicators.note: employed in means placed within, so is goes inside the trimmed word
mostly means not the whole, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: panto, pantomime, is the British Christmas stage show

explanation.surface: A boy drummer gets a part in the Christmas show.
explanation.walkthrough: PANTO (a British Christmas family show) loses its last letter by 'mostly' to give PANT, which IS goes into: PAN-IS-T.
explanation.definitionFit: A timpanist plays the kettledrums in an orchestra, a kind of drummer.

clue.text: Has hunch involving first of tips in northern race

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the plural people's name encloses the letter

parts.note: the Inuit are a people of the Arctic north

indicators.note: first of takes the opening letter of the word tips

explanation.surface: A punter has a hunch about a horse race, guided by tips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race' suggests horse racing but means a people, the Inuit; T goes inside: IN-T-UITS.
explanation.definitionFit: To intuit is to know by instinct, to have a hunch.

clue.text: Fairylike female trapped by rising river

indicators.note: trapped by means held within, so the letter goes inside the other piece
rising in a down clue means read upwards, so the river is reversed

parts.note: the Nile is the African river

explanation.surface: A woman caught by a flooding river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns NILE into ELIN, and F goes inside: EL-F-IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfin means like an elf, delicate and small like a fairy.

clue.text: Times of past triumphs happening originally in Bess's reign

indicators.note: originally means at the beginning, so the opening letters of the two words before it are taken

parts.note: in a monarch's reign is under that monarch; Bess is Elizabeth I, ER (Elizabeth Regina)

explanation.surface: A history of England's triumphs in Elizabeth I's time, written up in the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' takes TH from 'triumphs happening'; 'in Bess's reign' is UNDER ER. The Times of London was long nicknamed this for its thundering editorials.
explanation.definitionFit: The old nickname of the London newspaper, earned by its forceful editorials in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Correct to return, following second theme

indicators.note: following places the second-named piece after the first in the answer

parts.note: MO is short for moment, a second

indicators.note: to return means to go back, so the word for correct is read backwards

parts.note: fit means proper or correct

explanation.surface: An instruction to go back and correct the second theme of a piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' gives MO, short for 'moment', as in 'half a mo'; 'Correct' is the adjective meaning suitable, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring idea or theme in music, art or literature.

clue.text: Cheering up?

parts.note: read literally, it is applause given by people who are up on their feet, not the act of making someone happier

explanation.surface: A simple question about making someone feel better.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience rising to its feet to applaud is cheering while up off the seats.

clue.text: The old still amicable — head off for resort

indicators.note: read as re-sort, to sort again, so the remaining letters are rearranged
taking the head off removes the first letter of the word amicable

explanation.surface: An old distillery owner is friendly, then heads off for a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head off' drops the first A of 'amicable', leaving MICABLE, and 'resort' (re-sort) rearranges those letters. 'Still' looks like an adverb but is the distilling apparatus.
explanation.definitionFit: An alembic is an antique distilling apparatus, used by alchemists, so it is an old kind of still.

clue.text: Exotic bird heading East rightly creates a stir

indicators.note: exotic means strange or foreign, so the letters of the word bird are rearranged

parts.note: well can mean rightly or properly

explanation.surface: A rare bird flying east makes a commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' is slang for prison; Bridewell was a London prison whose name became general for a jail. 'heading' just sets E next.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir is slang for a jail, and a bridewell is an old term for a prison or house of correction.

clue.text: Fellow prepared to show matching knitwear

parts.note: a fellow is one of a pair, a counterpart, as is a twin
set means ready or prepared

explanation.surface: A man gets ready to show off his matching jumper and cardigan.
explanation.walkthrough: A twinset is a woman's matching jumper and cardigan, a classic British outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: The garment is a matching pair of knitted top and cardigan worn together.

clue.text: Fund manager needs to negotiate cut with more assurance

indicators.note: cut means shortened, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to treat is to negotiate terms
surer means more confident

explanation.surface: An investment manager has to negotiate cuts with greater confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' looks like a noun after 'negotiate', as in negotiating a pay cut, but it shortens the verb's synonym by its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasurer looks after the funds of a club or organisation.

clue.text: Sum laid out for both-ways speculation?

indicators.note: laid out means arranged afresh, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gambler lays out a sum on a bet that covers both outcomes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid' does double service only in the surface; in the wordplay it is fodder and 'out' with it signals the shuffle. Dualism holds two principles, mind and matter, hence 'both-ways' and the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Dualism is the philosophical view that reality has two fundamental kinds, so it is thinking in two directions.

clue.text: Stinginess in dishing out caviare

indicators.note: dishing out suggests serving up in a new arrangement, so the letters of caviare are rearranged

explanation.surface: Being mean when serving caviar to guests.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is greed for money, and meanness or stinginess goes with it.

clue.text: Changeable wind in first half of day, before long

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of the next
first half of takes the opening three of the six letters of the day name

parts.note: Monday is a day of the week
soon means before long

explanation.surface: The weather turns windy in the morning, and it won't be long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'long' gives SOON only with 'before': 'before long' is soon, but 'before' also orders the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A monsoon is a seasonal wind of South Asia that reverses direction with the seasons.

clue.text: Diplomat almost engaged

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the word for engaged is dropped

parts.note: someone attached is engaged or in a relationship

explanation.surface: A diplomat is almost engaged to be married.
explanation.definitionFit: An attaché is a junior member of an embassy's diplomatic staff.

clue.text: A cheat's rarely a faithful friend

indicators.note: rarely, in the sense of done rare or unusually, signals the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cheat is seldom a loyal companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Achates was Aeneas's loyal companion in Virgil's Aeneid; his name became a byword for a faithful friend.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Aeneid he is Aeneas's constant companion, known as 'fidus Achates', faithful Achates.

clue.text: Note rush to subdue

parts.note: C is a musical note
hasten means hurry or rush

explanation.surface: A memo urging people to hurry and quieten down.
explanation.definitionFit: To chasten is to restrain or humble someone, to subdue them.

clue.text: Grasp ass, perhaps, that's an undependable type

parts.note: the word grass with asp, a snake, set inside it gives the letters of grasp ass, so the phrase literally depicts a serpent among the grass

explanation.surface: Someone who would grab a donkey is not to be trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: GR(ASP)ASS spells 'Grasp ass': an asp, a snake, inside GRASS. 'perhaps' marks it as an example of the answer's idea.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a treacherous person who hides their hostility, like a hidden serpent.

clue.text: Firm promoted one internally

indicators.note: internally means on the inside, so the numeral goes inside

parts.note: sold can mean promoted, as an idea is sold
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A company promoted one of its staff from within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company but is the adjective; 'promoted' means persuaded people of, SOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Solid means firm and hard, not liquid or yielding.

clue.text: One of Alfred's successors, also bad cook

definitions.text: One of Alfred's successors, also bad cook

parts.words: One of Alfred's successors, also bad cook
parts.note: King Alfred legendarily burnt the cakes; a later burner of food, a heat source that can char things, is described as if it were a king following him

explanation.surface: A line from a history of English kings after Alfred the Great.
explanation.walkthrough: The legend of Alfred burning the cakes is a British schoolroom story; the device that browns food under fierce heat 'succeeds' him as a scorcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Food cooked under fierce direct heat can be charred like Alfred's cakes, so the cooking device follows his example.

clue.text: French runner between banks has nothing in Italian currency

indicators.note: in places the zero inside the word for the currency

parts.note: lire was the plural of lira, Italy's currency before the euro
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A French athlete with no money in Italian lire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runner' looks like an athlete but is a river, flowing between its banks; the banks sound financial too.
explanation.definitionFit: The Loire is France's longest river, which runs between its banks.

clue.text: Clothier who has dismissed tailor

parts.note: a batsman dismissed in cricket is out
a fitter is one who fits clothes, as a tailor does

explanation.surface: A clothes shop owner sacks the tailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismissed' looks like sacking the tailor, but it is the cricket sense: a batsman dismissed is out.
explanation.definitionFit: An outfitter sells clothing, so is a clothier.

clue.text: Houses duke with boots out of fashion

indicators.note: out of here means taken away from, so the word for fashion is removed

parts.note: wellingtons are rubber boots
ton is an old word for fashion, as in bon ton

explanation.surface: A duke whose boots have gone out of style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of fashion' looks like one phrase meaning outmoded, but it splits: 'out of' is the removal and 'fashion' is the old word ton, as in bon ton.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwellings are places where people live, as houses are.

clue.text: Left individual right behind, to become a recluse

indicators.note: behind puts the letter for right after the others

parts.note: one means a single individual

explanation.surface: Someone left behind by everyone becomes a hermit.
explanation.definitionFit: A loner prefers to be alone, like a hermit or recluse.
